newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia still has to make progress before EU talks.
newsitem.headline: Croatia still has to make progress before EU talks.

text.p: European parliament members said on Friday Croatia had made progress with the return of displaced people, but they were divided on whether it was time to restart negotiations on an agreement with the European Union.

"I think we should not give the impression that the European parliament is going to press unanimously for the restart of negotiations. We have very serious reservations," Giorgio La Malfa of Italy told Reuters after a news conference.
Negotiations on Croatia being included in a European Union assistance programme were suspended in August 1995 after a Croatian army offensive to retake Serb-occupied areas.
The so-called PHARE programme provides technical assistance to help central and eastern European countries establish democracies and market economies.
"You have to fulfil more conditions to be ready for the PHARE programme," Doris Pack, chairman of the European parliament's south east Europe delegation, told reporters.

"In the programme there are a lot of things which could be given to young people to help them to be better Europeans. We intend to speak to our people about giving some parts of this programme to help implement democracy (in Croatia)," she said.

La Malfa said he had "reservations from the findings of our mission, regarding refugees and co-ethnicity with Serbs, freedom of the press and concerning the way in which the presidential election took place in this country.
"All these things have to be considered very carefully before thinking of restarting the PHARE programme."
La Malfa said he was less enthusiastic than the rest of the delegation, made up of four members of the European Parliament including Pack from Germany and two Austrian representatives .

Croatia has made clear it wants to become a fully paid-up member of the EU and other Western institutions. It is under severe pressure from the United States to meet demands over human rights and the media if it is to win U.S. support.
European governments have been less outspoken, but many diplomats said there was still a long way to go before Croatia could be considered for EU membership.

Pack said the delegation had seen improvements during a visit to Eastern Slavonia, the last Serb enclave in Croatia. It is currently administered by the United Nations but is due to be reintegrated into Croatia under Zagreb rule next month.
Thousands of Serbs who fled the 1995 offensive settled in Eastern Slavonia. Around 5,000 of them want to return home but many houses are occupied by ethnic Croat refugees from Bosnia.
Some Serbs who have returned home were attacked by bitter Bosnian Croats who cannot envisage living beside their former foes. Some properties were burned down.
The European parliamentarians held their fifth meeting with members of Croatia's parliament, or Sabor, this week.
Pack said one concern the delegation raised was a law allowing the temporary takeover by the authorities of property owned by Serbs which was abandoned when they fled.
"Our colleagues said they are in favour of changing this law. It exists in a similar form in the Bosnian Serb Republic and the Croat-Moslem Federation (which constitute Bosnia)."

She said the law had to be changed in Bosnia and said she had asked Croatian politicians to use their influence in Croat areas of Bosnia to support the federation with Moslems. It was forged in 1994 and makes up 51 percent of Bosnia.

Pack also asked Croatian journalists to try and pressure the government to loosen its control over the media, which was heavily criticised in a report by international monitors for its one-sided coverage of the presidential election campaign.
